title: Teach These Things Freely unto Your Children
hook: Genesis 5 is more than a genealogy—it's a theological manifesto. Every name from Adam to Noah tells a story: "Adam" (man), "Seth" (appointed), "Enosh" (mortal), "Kenan" (sorrow), "Mahalalel" (the blessed God), "Jared" (shall come down), "Enoch" (teaching), "Methuselah" (his death shall bring), "Lamech" (despairing), "Noah" (rest/comfort). Read together, these names form a sentence: "Man [is] appointed mortal sorrow, [but] the blessed God shall come down teaching; His death shall bring the despairing rest." Before the flood narrative even begins, Genesis encodes the gospel of Jesus Christ into the very structure of human genealogy. This week, we encounter not just names and numbers, but the unbroken covenant line that preserved the plan of salvation through the darkest generations of apostasy.
overview:
Genesis 5 and Moses 6 form one continuous narrative that the King James Version artificially splits. Genesis 5 provides the skeletal genealogy from Adam to Noah, while Moses 6 (revealed through Joseph Smith) fills in the theological meat—showing us that Adam's descendants weren't primitive nomads groping in darkness, but a covenant people with temple ordinances, priesthood authority, a written language, and a "book of remembrance" recording revelations. The Joseph Smith Translation and Pearl of Great Price restore 52 verses to the Genesis account that were lost or removed, transforming our understanding of antediluvian religion from primitive myth to sophisticated covenant theology. Moses 6 reveals that Adam's posterity held councils, practiced baptism, received the Holy Ghost, and understood the Atonement with remarkable clarity. The repetition of "and he died" in Genesis 5 becomes less a drumbeat of mortality and more a testimony that each generation passed the covenant torch to the next, preserving priesthood keys through eight generations until Enoch could establish Zion and Noah could save the human family through the Flood. The question these chapters pose isn't "How could people live so long?" but "How did the gospel survive intact through centuries of wickedness?"

The centerpiece of Moses 6 is verses 48-68, where Adam receives the plan of salvation in its fullness. This is the Bible's clearest pre-Sinai articulation of covenant theology: repentance, baptism by water and fire, the gift of the Holy Ghost, justification, sanctification, and being "born again" into the family of Christ. Significantly, the Book of Moses reveals that this wasn't progressive revelation—Adam knew the name "Jesus Christ," understood the Atonement's mechanics, and taught his children "these things freely." The gospel was delivered complete at the beginning, not assembled piecemeal across centuries. This undermines any notion that ancient religion was primitive or that Christianity emerged from evolutionary religious development. Moses 6:57 contains one of scripture's most complete theological statements: "Therefore teach it unto your children, that all men, everywhere, must repent, or they can in nowise inherit the kingdom of God, for no unclean thing can dwell there, or dwell in his presence." This is Mosaic law, Pauline theology, and latter-day temple theology all present in the first generation. The ancient covenant wasn't simpler—it was the same.

Enoch's ministry, beginning in Moses 6:26-47, bridges the gap between Adam's Edenic dispensation and Noah's covenant. Called as a young man despite being "slow of speech," Enoch demonstrates that prophetic authority doesn't depend on natural eloquence but on divine anointing. His vision of the weeping God (Moses 7, next week) becomes one of scripture's most profound theodicies, but it's grounded in the practical reality Moses 6 establishes: Enoch walked with God because he first learned to teach the gospel plainly. The phrase "Enoch walked with God" (Genesis 5:24) becomes less mystical and more concrete in light of Moses 6—it means he lived the covenant so thoroughly that translation was the natural next step, not a miraculous exception. The Book of Moses reveals that multiple people in Enoch's city were translated, suggesting this was the designed outcome of living the gospel in its fullness. Our modern covenant path, with its emphasis on temple ordinances and enduring to the end, mirrors exactly what Enoch taught his people.

The Hebrew of Genesis 5 contains subtle linguistic treasures. The phrase "in the likeness of God made he him" (v. 1) uses the word "demuth" (likeness), the same word used in Genesis 1:26 for humanity's creation in God's image. The repetition emphasizes continuity—Seth was born in Adam's likeness (v. 3) just as Adam was created in God's likeness, establishing that the divine image passes generationally through covenant families. The name "Enosh" (v. 6) marks a theological watershed: it's the same word used in Genesis 4:26 when "men began to call upon the name of the Lord." This wasn't the first prayer—Adam prayed—but possibly the first organized, congregational worship as wickedness spread and the righteous became a distinct community. The ages recorded (Adam lived 930 years, Methuselah 969) aren't scribal errors or mythological inflation but likely reflect the pre-Flood environment's dramatically different conditions—which modern revelation confirms (D&C 77:6-7). These extended lifespans meant that Adam personally taught Methuselah for 243 years, ensuring doctrinal continuity across what would otherwise have been many generations.

The Restoration lens is essential for understanding Genesis 5 and Moses 6 because without the Joseph Smith Translation and Book of Moses, we're reading a gutted text. The JST restoration includes the gospel being preached to Adam (Moses 5:58-59), the ordinance of baptism being instituted (Moses 6:64-65), and the critical revelation that "by the water ye keep the commandment; by the Spirit ye are justified, and by the blood ye are sanctified" (Moses 6:60)—a complete articulation of the sacramental theology we practice today. These weren't innovations Joseph Smith invented; they were restorations of what ancient prophets taught. The Book of Mormon provides independent verification: Alma 13:1-9 speaks of a holy order "prepared from the foundation of the world," and 2 Nephi 31 teaches the doctrine of Christ in terms nearly identical to Moses 6. The temple connections are unmistakable—Adam built altars (Moses 5:5), his family kept sacred records (Moses 6:5-6), they used a "pure language" (Moses 6:6), and they gathered at a specific holy place called Adam-ondi-Ahman (D&C 107:53). This is temple-centered religion in every particular, centuries before Sinai. When President Joseph Fielding Smith taught that "the gospel in its fulness was revealed to Adam," he wasn't speculating—he was reading Moses 6.
themes: The Gospel Given Complete from the Beginning
The Book of Remembrance and Sacred Record-Keeping

key_verses.text_kjv: Wherefore teach it unto your children, that all men, everywhere, must repent, or they can in nowise inherit the kingdom of God, for no unclean thing can dwell there, or dwell in his presence; for, in the language of Adam, Man of Holiness is his name, and the name of his Only Begotten is the Son of Man, even Jesus Christ, a righteous Judge, who shall come in the meridian of time.
key_verses.insight: This verse contains more complete theology than most Old Testament books combined—repentance, universal atonement, sanctification requirements, the name "Jesus Christ" revealed to Adam, and even the timing of Christ's mortal ministry. Adam's dispensation wasn't a proto-gospel; it was the gospel in full. The phrase "in the language of Adam" suggests temple language, the pure communication that transcends cultural and linguistic barriers.

key_verses.text_kjv: And Enoch said unto the Lord: Why is it that I have found favor in thy sight, and am but a lad, and all the people hate me; for I am slow of speech; wherefore am I thy servant?
key_verses.insight: Enoch's self-doubt echoes Moses, Jeremiah, and every reluctant prophet. The Lord's answer (v. 32): "Go forth and do as I have commanded thee"—no special eloquence granted, just divine backing. This is the pattern of prophetic calls: God doesn't remove weakness but rather consecrates it. Enoch's "slow of speech" complaint makes his later linguistic power ("the mountains fled before him") all the more remarkable.

key_verses.text_kjv: And Enoch walked with God: and he was not; for God took him.
key_verses.insight: This terse KJV description becomes monumental in Moses 7—Enoch didn't just disappear, he and his entire city were translated. The phrase "walked with God" isn't mystical metaphor but covenant description: Enoch lived the principles that qualified him and his people for translation. The same phrase describes Noah (Genesis 6:9), suggesting this was the expected outcome of covenant faithfulness, not a rare exception.

key_verses.text_kjv: For by the water ye keep the commandment; by the Spirit ye are justified, and by the blood ye are sanctified; therefore it is given to abide in you; the record of heaven; the Comforter; the peaceable things of immortal glory; the truth of all things; that which quickeneth all things, which maketh alive all things; that which knoweth all things, and hath all power according to wisdom, mercy, truth, justice, and judgment.
key_verses.insight: This verse maps the entire covenant path: baptism (water), receiving the Holy Ghost (Spirit), and being cleansed through Christ's atonement (blood). The description of the Holy Ghost's role contains some of scripture's richest theological language—"the record of heaven," "the truth of all things," "that which quickeneth all things." What we teach in missionary discussions and temple instruction was revealed to Adam in its completeness.

key_verses.text_kjv: And a book of remembrance was kept, in the which was recorded, in the language of Adam, for it was given unto as many as called upon God to write by the spirit of inspiration; And by them their children were taught to read and write, having a language which was pure and undefiled.
key_verses.insight: The notion that early humans were illiterate primitives collapses here. Adam's descendants kept written records in a "pure and undefiled" language, taught reading and writing systematically, and wrote "by the spirit of inspiration"—suggesting these were sacred texts, not merely genealogical lists. This is the origin of scripture itself: covenant people recording revelation for their children. Every scripture we read continues this pattern started in Adam's generation.

highlights.snippet_text: The Hebrew word 'demuth' (likeness) appears in both verse 1 (humanity created in God's likeness) and verse 3 (Seth born in Adam's likeness), creating a genealogical chain of divine image. This isn't metaphorical—ancient readers understood that covenant families literally transmitted sacred characteristics generationally, making genealogy a theological matter, not just record-keeping.
highlights.label: Hebrew Insight

highlights.snippet_text: The JST reveals that baptism wasn't introduced by John the Baptist but was practiced from Adam: "Therefore I give unto you a commandment, to teach these things freely unto your children... and ye shall be baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son... and by the Holy Ghost." The identical formula we use today was given in the first generation—baptism is as old as humanity.
highlights.label: Restoration Insight

highlights.snippet_text: Adam knew the name "Jesus Christ" and taught it to his children—a detail that astounds readers expecting progressive revelation. This aligns perfectly with King Benjamin's teaching that "there shall be no other name given" (Mosiah 5:8) and Jacob's testimony that prophets "knew of Christ, and had a hope of his glory" (Jacob 4:4). The gospel message hasn't evolved; it's been the same from the beginning.
highlights.label: Cross-Reference

highlights.snippet_text: Adam's question—"Why is it that men must repent and be baptized in water?"—receives the answer that all must be "born again into the kingdom of heaven, of water, and of the Spirit." President Ezra Taft Benson taught that being born again isn't a single dramatic event but the ongoing process of covenant living. Adam's experience establishes the pattern: covenant, ordinance, transformation, teaching the next generation.
highlights.label: Prophetic Connection

highlights.snippet_text: Methuselah lived 969 years—the longest recorded human lifespan. His name means "his death shall bring," and remarkably, he died the year of the flood (Genesis 5:27 records his age; Genesis 7:6 records Noah's age at the flood; the math aligns perfectly). This suggests Methuselah's life was a divine mercy, delaying judgment until the last righteous patriarch passed. God's patience with the wicked extended for nearly a millennium.
highlights.label: Historical Context

highlights.snippet_text: Adam's descendants taught their children "to read and write, having a language which was pure and undefiled." This challenges our assumption that ancient people were less sophisticated, but more importantly, it models covenant parenting: literacy, sacred texts, deliberate religious instruction. The pattern isn't accidental—every dispensation preserves the gospel through parents teaching children. Our homes are the continuation of Adam's book of remembrance.
highlights.label: Modern Application

restoration_lens:
The Joseph Smith Translation's contribution to Genesis 5 and Moses 6 cannot be overstated—without it, we'd have a genealogy and little else. With it, we have a complete theology of covenant religion practiced from humanity's beginning. The JST restores 52 verses to this section, including the entire structure of Adam's gospel instruction (Moses 5:58-59), the institution of baptism (Moses 6:52-68), the role of the Holy Ghost in justification and sanctification (Moses 6:60), and the establishment of sacred record-keeping (Moses 6:4-8). These aren't peripheral additions; they're the theological core that ancient apostasy or careless transmission stripped away. Joseph Smith didn't invent the idea that Adam was baptized—he restored the ancient account that testified of it. The Book of Mormon provides independent witness: Nephi saw in vision that "plain and precious things" were removed from early biblical records (1 Nephi 13:26-29), and the Moses account shows us precisely what was lost. When Alma teaches that God ordained priests "from the foundation of the world" (Alma 13:3) and Jacob testifies that ancient prophets "truly testified of" Christ (Jacob 7:11), they're describing the religion of Moses 6, not speculating about primitive faith.

The Doctrine and Covenants adds geographical and administrative specificity to these early events. Section 107:53-57 reveals that three years before Adam's death, he gathered his righteous posterity at a place called Adam-ondi-Ahman in Daviess County, Missouri—where he gave them his final blessing and where Christ will meet with priesthood leaders in preparation for His second coming. This isn't folklore; it's revealed geography linking ancient covenant history to modern Missouri. Section 78:16 refers to this council as an organizational meeting of priesthood authority, suggesting early Christianity's organization (apostles, seventies, high priests) was a restoration of Adam's order, not an innovation. Section 84:16 traces the priesthood lineage from Moses back through Abraham, Melchizedek, and ultimately to Adam, who "obtained the First Presidency" and held keys directly from Christ (D&C 107:40-42). This priesthood continuity, preserved through Enoch, Methuselah, and Noah, is the backbone of Genesis 5's genealogy—it's not just biological descent but priesthood succession. President Joseph Fielding Smith taught explicitly: "The gospel in its fulness was revealed to Adam... It has been the same in all dispensations." This isn't theological opinion; it's reading Moses 6 plainly.

The temple connections are woven throughout. Adam's building of altars (Moses 5:5), the gathering of his posterity for instruction (Moses 6:1-2), the sacred language in which they communicated (Moses 6:6), and the instruction in covenants and ordinances all parallel modern temple practice. The phrase "language which was pure and undefiled" echoes the temple's transcendent communication, where meaning surpasses mere words. Elder Bruce R. McConkie noted that temple language "views things through spiritual eyes" and that Adam's pure language represented prelapsarian clarity about divine things. The book of remembrance wasn't a diary—it was scripture, revelation recorded for covenant instruction, exactly what happens when apostles and prophets write under inspiration today. Our modern emphasis on family history and temple ordinances continues Adam's pattern: connecting generations, preserving covenant identity, and preparing families for exaltation. When we attend the temple, we participate in the same ordinance structure Adam received: washings, anointings, covenants, and instruction in God's purposes. Moses 6 is, fundamentally, a temple text.
application:
For modern Latter-day Saints navigating secular culture, Moses 6's message is radical: you are not innovating a new religion or clinging to outdated tradition—you are continuing the faith delivered to Adam, the pure gospel that predates every human institution. When society dismisses religious commitment as evolutionary artifact, Moses 6 testifies that covenant religion is older than civilization itself, deliberately delivered by God to the first humans. The doctrine we teach our children in family home evening—faith, repentance, baptism, the Holy Ghost, enduring to the end—is precisely what Adam taught his children. This should embolden covenant members to teach "these things freely unto your children" (Moses 6:58) without embarrassment or apology. We're not imposing our values on neutral children; we're introducing them to the faith structure humanity was designed to receive. The pressure parents feel to soften doctrine, to make the gospel more palatable to modern sensibilities, dissolves when you recognize that the gospel wasn't constructed to fit cultural preferences—it's the revealed pattern for human flourishing, unchanged since Eden. Teach baptism. Teach the Fall and Atonement. Teach Christ's name. You're doing exactly what Adam did.

For those struggling with faith, Moses 6 offers unexpected comfort: even Enoch, who would build Zion and be translated, began by saying, "I am but a lad, and all the people hate me; for I am slow of speech" (Moses 6:31). The man who later commanded mountains felt inadequate and unlikable. The Lord's response wasn't to remove Enoch's weaknesses but to send him anyway: "Go forth and do as I have commanded thee, and no man shall pierce thee" (Moses 6:32). Modern members wrestling with inadequacy, feeling unequal to their callings or drowning in self-doubt, should find profound hope here. God doesn't wait until you feel capable—He calls you while you're weak, precisely so His power can be manifest in your service. Enoch's transformation from "slow of speech" to a prophet whose words made mountains flee happened not through self-improvement seminars but through obedient action. The pattern is consistent: covenant living, even by the inadequate, produces transformation that self-help never could. If you're serving in a calling that feels too big, teaching children who aren't listening, or trying to minister to people who seem uninterested—you're in Enoch's position. Keep teaching. Keep serving. Transformation comes through persistence, not charisma.

Finally, Genesis 5's genealogy, with its drumbeat of "and he died," poses the uncomfortable question: what legacy are we leaving? Adam lived 930 years, Seth 912, Enosh 905—and each one died. Despite centuries of life, mortality claimed them. Yet their faithfulness ensured that Noah, ten generations later, had the gospel intact. The book of remembrance they kept (Moses 6:5) preserved revelations that would eventually reach us. Every journal entry, every family scripture study, every testimony shared with children is part of that same record-keeping. We are writing our own books of remembrance, whether in leather journals or digital documents, and our children's faith may depend on what we record. The sobering reality is that most of Genesis 5's listed patriarchs are names without stories—we know their ages but not their struggles, their conversion moments, their doubts and triumphs. Only Enoch gets narrative space because his story was recorded in detail. What parts of your spiritual journey are you documenting? What revelations, tender mercies, or answered prayers are you preserving for your posterity? Covenant record-keeping isn't narcissism; it's responsibility. Future generations need to know how you found faith, how you endured trials, how you encountered Christ. Like Adam's book of remembrance, your record may be the thread that keeps the gospel intact through difficult generations ahead.
